candidates.title: Partisan responsiveness in real time: causal evidence from Trump’s military attack on Iran
candidates.abstract: Abstract Elite cues signal citizens how to interpret political events through a partisan lens. Do these effects occur in real time? We exploit President Trump’s unexpected announcement of US military strikes against Iran during a nationally representative survey to estimate the causal effect of elite cues on public opinion. Leveraging minute-level variation in exposure, we find that partisan divergence emerges almost immediately: support for military intervention increases among Republicans but declines among Democrats. These large effects remain robust across 28,672 model specifications and 57,344 partisan-specific treatment effects. Our quasi-experimental evidence demonstrates that elite cues can polarize public opinion within minutes, even before media framing and partisan commentary have diffused, highlighting the speed of partisan opinion formation and its implications for democratic accountability.

candidates.title: Beyond technocracy: Toward a holistic approach to central bank trust
candidates.abstract: We examine public trust in the European Central Bank (ECB) and its correlates using survey data from the Bundesbank Online Panel of Households for Germany. Drawing on insights from political science and psychology, we move beyond technocracy and develop a more holistic account of central bank trust. We show that trust in the ECB is associated with both competence aspects, defined as effectiveness in maintaining price stability and reliance on rules, scientific analysis and data—and value aspects, particularly the integrity of senior policymakers, honest communication and broader societal concern. Respondents who report that competence matters more report significantly higher trust in the ECB. In contrast, those who place greater importance on values tend to express lower trust. Trust in the ECB is also strongly associated with trust in political institutions more generally and, to a lesser extent, interpersonal trust. Together, our findings offer a fresh perspective on trust in central banks, in which respondents report value-related considerations alongside competence. Integrity and transparent communication are already part of the ECB’s existing ethics and accountability framework, so placing weight on these considerations raises no question about its mandate.

candidates.title: Beliefs About Public Opinion and the Perceived Legitimacy of Policy Decisions
candidates.abstract: Abstract Democratic legitimacy is typically thought to depend on whether political decisions reflect public opinion, or majority preferences. Do citizens share this standard? And what if citizens are wrong about public opinion? We study how beliefs about public support for controversial policy proposals are associated with the perceived legitimacy of adopting them, and whether accurate polling information changes these judgments. In a representative survey experiment in Germany, respondents reported their own position on four such proposals, estimated public support, and rated the legitimacy of adopting each one. For a random subset of proposals, respondents received accurate polling information showing that the proposal lacked majority support. We find that perceived public support predicts legitimacy judgments even after accounting for respondents’ own policy preferences. Yet these perceptions are often inaccurate and shaped by respondents’ own views. Corrective polling information modestly lowers perceived legitimacy, especially among those who initially overestimated public support. The findings suggest that misperceptions of public opinion can distort, but accurate information can also partly correct, citizens’ assessments of democratic legitimacy.

candidates.title: Learning traps
candidates.abstract: Abstract When constituents are uncertain about whether leaders' policy preferences align with their interests, policy choices generate a trade‐off between payoffs and information. Leaders can experiment with their preferred policy, but if the outcome is bad, constituents learn this and threaten office removal. I use a repeated model of political agency to analyze how this trade‐off shapes long‐lived, term‐unlimited leaders' policy choices. When there is uncertainty about the optimal policy for constituents, leaders implement “learning traps”: spatially intermediate policies that halt learning about what the best policy is. They experiment only when their preferences are very likely to be aligned with constituents, a contrast to the “gambling for resurrection” logic ubiquitous in the literature. I provide a case study that examines how the 1861 reforms ending Serfdom in Imperial Russia represented the logic of a “learning trap” and illustrate additional applications of the model to political contagion and economic policymaking.

candidates.title: Economic Self-Interest and Support for Redistribution: New Evidence Using Election Results Data
candidates.abstract: A formidable corpus of scholarship explores the role of economic self-interest in shaping public support for redistribution. One striking feature of this literature is its near-exclusive reliance on reported preferences in surveys, with little-to-no research analyzing revealed preferences in the form of actual voting on redistribution. Leveraging eight redistributive ballot initiatives across six American states and a total of 73,053 observations of revealed support for redistribution, we uncover consistent evidence that the economic standing of precinct voters is systematically related to their support for redistribution. We find that lower- to upper-middle-income precincts are each significantly more supportive of redistribution than upper-income precincts, with pronounced decreases in support associated with the increasing prevalence of high-income households subject to proposed tax increases. Finally, we observe the largest class differential in support for redistribution in more heavily Republican precincts.

candidates.title: Host-country media discourse and China’s economic presence in Africa
candidates.abstract: China’s economic engagement in Africa takes place in changing host-country discourse environments, yet the consequences of adverse media reporting for China’s overseas presence remain unclear. We argue that worsening media tone can signal rising operating risk and may therefore trigger adjustment across different margins of presence. Using an annual panel of 54 African countries for 2010–2023, we construct lagged media-tone shocks from the Global Database of Events, Language, and Tone and estimate their dynamic association with Chinese project personnel and FDI stocks. We combine Double Machine Learning with two-way fixed effects, conventional fixed-effects benchmarks, balanced-sample checks and an Afrobarometer exercise. The evidence is consistent with a selective-adjustment pattern. Negative media-tone shocks are associated with a delayed reduction in Chinese project personnel, with effects that emerge at the three- and four-year horizons. Positive shocks show no comparable expansion effect. Chinese overseas presence adjusts primarily to negative shifts in discourse through the more flexible personnel margin, while FDI stocks respond slowly and less consistently. The host country’s institutional context also influences the staffing response. The findings suggest that hostile discourse becomes especially materially consequential when it is likely to translate into operating risk.

candidates.title: Trading migration? Explaining mobility provisions in preferential trade agreements
candidates.abstract: Abstract Notwithstanding a generally unfavorable political climate regarding international migration, preferential trade agreements (PTAs) increasingly include provisions facilitating the temporary movement of specific categories of workers. Today, approximately seven in ten newly concluded PTAs contain clauses that enable the mobility of workers and businesspeople—particularly business visitors and intra-corporate transferees, who constitute a substantial share of skilled temporary migration in advanced industrial economies. This trend is striking given states’ longstanding emphasis on preserving sovereign control over migration policy. This article investigates the drivers of mobility provisions in PTAs and the implications for broader economic and migration policy. We develop and test three theoretical logics: (1) a trade logic grounded in interests resulting from economic interdependence; (2) a politics logic centered on migration control objectives; and (3) an institutional logic emphasizing path dependence and diffusion. Drawing on the MITA dataset, which codes mobility provisions in PTAs globally from 1960 to 2020, we find that economic interdependence and institutional path dependence are the primary forces behind mobility provisions, while migration control prerogatives have little explanatory power for either the presence, scope, or depth of these provisions. Our findings underscore the economic rationale behind mobility provisions in trade agreements, highlighting a pattern of selective liberalization for highly skilled workers and an increasingly fragmented landscape of migration governance.

candidates.title: International Law, Republican Experiments, and Political Economy in the Americas
candidates.abstract: The most ambitious book under review, Greg Grandin's America, América, is a beautifully written narrative about the international relations of the Western Hemisphere.Grandin's plot centers on the development of "American international law," a body of norms and international law that exalts the sovereignty and well-being of nation-states.Grandin sees it begin to emerge with Bartolomé de las Casas (1474-1566), the Spanish Dominican priest who denounced the destruction of Indigenous peoples, and the professors and jurists at and around the University of Salamanca who developed theologies and legal theories to protect the rights of the original inhabitants of the Americas.Grandin's tale culminates with the hemispheric solidarity of World War II, when New Dealers, "who treated Latin America tenderly," argued that "the best way to advance democracy" was to combat "the fascist defenders of the oligarchy," and to increase "raising of wages and provision of welfare" (512).
institutions: University of North Carolina at Greensboro

candidates.title: Investigating the Utility of LLM-Based “Silicon Samples” in Political Science Conjoint Experiments
candidates.abstract: Abstract This research note is the first study to explore the viability of using LLM-generated respondents in forced-choice conjoint experiments. I generate naive “silicon samples” using three models, GPT 4o-Mini, Llama 3.2, and Magistral-small-2506, benchmarked to a large sample of live conjoint respondents, allowing for direct comparisons between human and silicon choices. The resulting analyses suggest that naively generated silicon samples are insufficient to simulate human decision-making in conjoint tasks; these results also suggest that there are systemic differences in the way demographic covariates shape LLM and human choices in experimental contexts. In total, this analysis makes two important contributions: it establishes a descriptive baseline understanding of LLM-generated respondent performance in conjoint experiments and suggests that naive silicon samples cannot accurately infer human choices using demographic traits in experimental decision making contexts. Finally, the implications of these results imply that LLMs consider covariates differently than live respondents do in micro-level decision making contexts.

candidates.title: Trade Interdependence in the Modern Global Economy
candidates.abstract: Analyzing global trade interdependence requires an approach that incorporates fundamental features of the modern economy: intense trade in intermediates and the changing availability of alternative partners and substitute products. We use theoretical models of structural gravity to construct measures of dyadic dependence that directly incorporate these features. The measures describe (1) how much trade interruptions damage a country’s welfare and (2) how much additional trade it would take from their existing trade partners to compensate. We then show three important findings. First, the new measures differ from traditional measures based on aggregate trade statistics. Second, they show how, contrary to much common wisdom, the world has not marched inexorably toward greater interdependence. Third, we use China’s foreign assistance, as exemplified by the Belt and Road Initiative, to assess the consequences of one major government policy. Chinese assistance has increased partners’ dependence on China, without a reciprocal increase in Chinese dependence.

Pursuing fiscal credibility, performing fiscal discipline: epistemic politics and status seeking in Italy and Spain’s Eurozone accession
candidates.abstract: There is a prolific literature on the politics of austerity, highlighting how its confidence effects arise from fiscal retrenchment embodying and signalling a credible commitment to markets’ interests. However, I argue that this implicitly performative account of fiscal credibility is too functionalist, underplaying how states continually negotiate it with different audiences. To overcome these issues, this article develops an alternative theorisation of (fiscal) credibility as a perlocutionary performative, meaning it is dependent on felicitous conditions to be brought about. Channelling a ‘practice-based constructivist’ framework through an ‘epistemic politics’ and ‘status seeking’ lens, I use archival and biographical research to study Italy and Spain’s Eurozone accession during the 1990s. My argument is that the success of their austerity programmes, and therefore of their accession strategies, depended on a series of cognitive and strategic dynamics beyond fiscal retrenchment – mainly, based on the epistemic politics of multilateral surveillance, national status claims to fiscal credibility, and the social construction of ‘credibility’ under a broad set of fiscal and non-fiscal parameters. As such, this article contributes to recent constructivist research on the practical life of ideas and on epistemic politics, showing the dynamics of construction, performance, and contestation surrounding austerity and fiscal credibility.

candidates.title: Can citizen election observation increase public confidence in US elections?
candidates.abstract: Abstract Nonpartisan citizen election observation plays an important role in promoting the credibility of electoral processes around the world. This article assesses whether nonpartisan observation can shape attitudes among the US public, randomizing information about nonpartisan domestic observers in a series of survey experiments fielded to nearly 10,000 respondents. These included both hypothetical vignettes and information about a real‐world nonpartisan domestic observation mission undertaken by The Carter Center during the 2022 midterm elections in Fulton County, Georgia. The results show that information about positive assessments by nonpartisan observers of the hypothetical and Fulton County elections increased respondents' confidence in electoral results and processes, and also made respondents more likely to identify the officially announced winner over the candidate they favored as the candidate who won. Alternative ways of framing observers were largely inconsequential.

candidates.title: When Can Political Parties Credibly Change Their Policies?
candidates.abstract: When can a party credibly change its policy on an issue? No institution forces parties to keep their promises after being elected. Voters may thus view platform shifts as mere pandering, discounting their credibility. We propose that voters use the direction of a platform shift as a signal of the party’s motives and policy commitment. Shifting to an unpopular position is a costly signal of principled motives, while moving toward a popular one suggests opportunistic ones. Two preregistered survey experiments, one evaluating a general setting and another focusing on a real case of mainstream party accommodation to the radical right, show that voters infer party motives and commitment from platform shifts in line with the predictions of our argument. Our study provides important insights into the electoral persistence of radical right parties, party system stability, and why platform shifts often fail to affect voter perceptions of party positions.

candidates.title: Distinction Without a Difference: American Public Opinion on Immigrants and Refugees
candidates.abstract: Abstract Do Americans hold refugees in higher regard than immigrants? If so, why? We theorize that refugees activate humanitarian concerns and perceptions of deservingness, while immigrants trigger threat perceptions and competition, leading to divergent mental associations toward each group. We investigate these questions with a nationally representative online survey experiment fielded in 2024 that contrasts Americans’ attitudes toward refugees and immigrants using both open- and close-ended questions. Open-ended mentions reveal that refugees trigger themes of involuntariness, conflict, and humanitarianism, while immigrants elicit themes of domestic politics, fairness, and threat. Close-ended responses indicate that Americans view immigrants as more competent and more agentic than refugees, and they associate refugees and immigrants with different reasons for coming to the United States. Despite these differences in beliefs, respondents report no significant differences on warmth stereotypes, group affect, or policy preferences. Thus, while Americans do possess some divergent beliefs about refugees and immigrants, ultimately these are distinctions without a difference when it comes to group affect and policy opinions.

candidates.title: Globalization unravelling? ASML and the geopolitics of Europe-China tech decoupling
candidates.abstract: This article investigates the geopolitical dynamics driving Europe’s emerging technological decoupling from China. Focusing on the semiconductor industry and the Dutch semiconductor firm ASML, it examines how technonationalism emanating from the US has shaped a small European member state’s policy response amid intensifying US-China rivalry. The article analyses how national security arguments and US strategic influence aimed at undermining China’s advances in high-tech has reshaped the Dutch semiconductor export control regime in a way that seemingly contradicts both ASML’s corporate interests and Dutch long-term economic interests. Moreover, cutting the dependency ties of China to one of the few chokepoint industries and tech firms in the EU arguably undermines its commitment to ‘technological sovereignty’. We explain these puzzling outcomes through the inherent contradictions within technonationalism and the tensions between state and corporate actors strategizing around different national security and profit-oriented interests. As such, we argue that the case of ASML offers a useful prism through which to study the ongoing ‘geoeconomic’ shift in the global political economy in which the alignment of the geopolitical and capital logics characteristic of neoliberal globalisation is coming apart, with state and corporate actors attempting to realign these logics into different configurations.

candidates.title: The semi-periphery's ‘defence dividend’: redistribution of labour in Europe's defence industry
candidates.abstract: The ramp up of European defence industrial production raises a critical question for the future shape and competitiveness of the European Defence Technological and Industrial Base (EDTIB): will it continue to be dominated and limited by core European Union (EU) producers or is there an ongoing redistribution of defence production? We argue a significant redistribution is underway, although not caused by recent geopolitical shocks, but by the long-term agency of the semi-periphery itself. Our analysis identifies a distinct long-term pathway of defence-industrial upgrading in Eastern and Central Europe (ECE), which unfolds within the broader context of Dependent Market Economies (DMEs) and which we term the Militarised DME (M-DME). The EU’s recent geoeconomic turn did not create this trajectory but validated and accelerated it. Using time-series cluster analysis of EU arms export data, we identify a sustained rise in high-value-added (HVA) exports associated primarily with indigenously controlled actors. Ultimately, our findings point to a contested re-division of labour that predates the current security crisis and has important implications for European strategic autonomy, industrial integration, and the future shape of the EDTIB.

candidates.title: Globalised but divided: European corporations and the EU’s geoeconomic turn against China
candidates.abstract: The European Union’s ‘geoeconomic turn’ against China is hotly debated among international political economy scholars, but the role of Europe’s leading corporations in this shift remains underexplored. This article focuses on the European Round Table for Industry, an elite forum of corporate executives tightly connected to the European Commission. The ERT played a key role in aligning European integration with corporate interests from the 1980s to 2000s. However, it has fallen out of step with the European Commission, whose posture has hardened since branding China a ‘systemic rival’. The disjuncture between the Commission’s assertive stance and the ERT’s more tentative approach to China prompts us to test and rethink what we know about state-business relations in a new geoeconomic age. Drawing on data under-used in IPE to chart ERT firms’ ‘territorial’ and ‘network integration’ with China, our analysis reveals a significant minority of firms deeply integrated into the Chinese market and supplier base, a small group of firms with minimal ties potentially receptive to the EU’s ‘geoeconomic turn’, and a large array of partially integrated companies in between these two positions. This uneasy balance of forces within the ERT explains why it is trailing rather than driving the EU’s stance.

candidates.title: Sustained Higher Education Expansion and Firms' Productivity: Evidence From China
candidates.abstract: ABSTRACT This study investigates the relationship between China's sustained higher education expansion and the productivity of A‐share listed firms from 2004 to 2020. We find that a larger supply of university graduates is associated with significantly higher firm total factor productivity (TFP) on average, a result robust to extensive testing. Mechanism analysis points to three plausible channels: an increased share of skilled labor, strengthened innovation, and accelerated digital transformation. However, the relationship is asymmetric. While graduate inflows are linked to higher TFP in large, R&D‐intensive, and high‐intangible‐asset firms, they are linked to lower productivity in small firms. Specifically, this negative association is concentrated among small enterprises that are non‐state‐owned, labor‐intensive, and financially constrained, with low intangible assets. These findings provide new micro‐level evidence on the heterogeneous value of human capital, offering policy implications for better alignment of graduate supply with firm capabilities.

candidates.title: Globalization and the Hinterland: International Trade and the Rural–Urban Divide
candidates.abstract: The growing political divide between rural and urban regions is often attributed to rural deindustrialization and import competition in manufacturing. Yet this cleavage emerged in many countries well before rural industrialization, pointing to underlying economic forces that existing accounts have overlooked. We argue that comparative advantage in agriculture is one such force: rural voters are more likely to support protectionist parties and policies when local agriculture is uncompetitive, as this sector is often central to their communities' economic and social life. Using a new harmonized dataset of surveys from 127 countries and extensive data on voting behavior, we find strong support for our argument. An additional analysis exploiting exogenous subnational variation in agricultural competitiveness in the United States post-NAFTA further corroborates our findings: The political divide between rural and urban voters is pronounced in uncompetitive regions but negligible in those possessing a comparative advantage in agriculture.

candidates.title: Post-National Tangos: Exile and Cultural Legitimation in El pretexto de París (Jorge Asís, 1985) and Informe de París (Paula Wajsman, 1990)
candidates.abstract: Abstract This article examines two novels that drew on the themes and tropes of tango to depict Argentine exile in Paris in the aftermath of the 1976–1983 dictatorship: Jorge Asís’s El pretexto de París (1985) and Paula Wajsman’s Informe de París (1990). These novels fictionalized Paris through the lens of Argentine culture to present controversial standpoints regarding issues that were heatedly debated at the time, such as the figure of the exiled intellectual and human rights activism. Moreover, both Asís and Wajsman designed their main characters and self-representations as authors by reimagining the gender archetypes of tango in the Parisian context. A cultural form particular to the Río de la Plata, tango allowed them to challenge the paradigm of the Latin American author favored in Europe during the 1980s, which was commonly associated with political commitment and the figures of the Boom. On the one hand, Asís reappropriated the opportunism and artfulness of the compadrito through a sexualized use of language that allegorized his masculine conquest of literary prestige. On the other hand, Wajsman reimagined the figure of the milonguita to reaffirm her independence as a woman and subvert gendered and neocolonial forms of cultural recognition.

candidates.title: Confronting Gender-Based Violence: Attacks on Women’s Organizations in Central America
candidates.abstract: Abstract Women’s rights organizations in Central America have been key actors in promoting women’s right to a life free of violence and advocating for reproductive rights and other social and economic protections for women and girls. Yet throughout Central America, these organizations have experienced myriad attacks in recent years. In this article, we examine attacks on women’s rights organizations in four Central American countries: Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, and Nicaragua. Although there are important distinctions among the regimes of these four countries, across all of them, setbacks for women have occurred in contexts characterized by increased militarization, autocratic governance, the incursion of conservative religious ideologies in government policies, and the spread of dangerous misinformation that discredits women’s organizations’ efforts. Within these regimes, women’s organizations have been subjected to intimidation, physical violence, legal threats, and digital harassment. Our analysis identifies patterns in these attacks, showing similarities and differences across the four countries during various temporal moments. To do so, we draw on twenty-nine interviews with twenty-eight women activists, academics, and human rights defenders in the region as well as a compilation of newspaper articles, social media, and independent reports documenting attacks on women’s rights leaders and organizations in the four countries. Efforts to dismantle the work of women’s organizations and committed feminists in Central America provide a window into the gendered dimensions of authoritarian practices in the region.

candidates.title: Breaking the Ice: Contributions and Challenges for Andean Glaciological Research Led by Women
candidates.abstract: Abstract This study examines the participation of women in Andean glaciology over the past four decades, combining a bibliometric analysis of 204 peer-reviewed articles (1983–2022) and a survey of female first authors (2018–2022). Results show a steady increase in women-led publications, rising from 8 percent in the 1980s–1990s to 30 percent in the past decade. However, structural barriers, including unequal access to funding, resistance to female leadership, and the disproportionate burden of caregiving, continue to limit gender equity in the field. Women-led studies are concentrated in Argentina and Chile, while countries like Colombia, Bolivia, and Venezuela remain underrepresented. The methods most commonly used by female researchers are fieldwork and remote sensing, which reflects limited access to laboratory-based approaches. Survey responses highlight both the motivations (scientific interest, conservation) and challenges (discrimination, lack of recognition, work-life imbalance) faced by women scientists. The findings reveal persistent epistemic and territorial asymmetries, especially in the context of international research led by Global North institutions. The study underscores the need for inclusive policies that go beyond formal representation, supporting equitable research leadership and collaboration. Promoting gender equity in cryosphere science is not only a matter of justice; it is essential for generating contextually relevant, socially just, and scientifically robust responses to climate change in the Andes.
